title: Where to Get the Best Ice Cream in Sonoma County
summary:
Whether it's hot, cold or somewhere in between, it's always a good time for ice cream. Here are the best places to get a cool, sweet scoop in Sonoma County.

The post Where to Get the Best Ice Cream in Sonoma County appeared first on Sonoma Magazine.
content:
Whether the weather’s hot, cold or somewhere in between, there’s never a bad time for ice cream. From swirls of soft serve and sorbet to traditional scoops and creamy custard, everyone’s got a favorite flavor.

Are you a strawberry waffle cone, lemon sorbet in a cup or chocolate and vanilla swirl in a cone? But the real question is, would you dare to eat pickle sorbet?

Whatever your choice, Sonoma County ice cream shops have you covered.

Top 15 Picks: Our Dining Editor’s Choices

Nimble & Finn’s, Santa Rosa and Guerneville

Cheeky by-the-scoop flavors include Front Porch Mint Chip (the mint is from one of the owner’s front porch), Meyer Lemon, Lavender Honeycomb and Whiskey Butterscotch. Can’t decide? Go for an eight-mini-scoop sampler. 16290 Main St., Guerneville, 707-666-9411; 123 Fourth St., Santa Rosa, 707-666-9590, nimbleandfinns.com

Goguette Bread, Santa Rosa

While known for their mélange of breads and pastries, Goguette also churns out delightful, French-style ice cream, or glacée. Using locally sourced or imported (from France and Italy) ingredients, find flavors like pear, lemon, chocolate orange, Madagascar vanilla and more. The bakery also sells ice cream cakes, with such flavors as vanilla, strawberry, pistachio and matcha. 59 Montgomery Drive, Santa Rosa, goguettebread.com

Handline, Sebastopol

This restaurant in Sebastopol was built on the site of an old Foster’s Freeze and the swirled chocolate and vanilla soft serve is still a favorite. Don’t miss the affogato, made with eye-opening cold brew and soft serve. 935 Gravenstein Highway S., Sebastopol, 707-827-3744, handline.com

Darling Ice Cream Shop, Sonoma

The ever-changing flavors at this charming Sonoma ice cream shop mean you’ll have plenty of reasons to return. A sister location to Sweet Scoops on the Sonoma Plaza, this neighborhood fave is known for its Watmaugh strawberry, salted caramel and, if you want to go the soft-serve route, a sunny Pineapple Dole Whip. 201 W. Napa St., Suite 6, Sonoma. 707-343-1482, darlingsonoma.com

Dave’s Gourmet Ice Cream, Santa Rosa

This local artisan producer uses premium organic milk, organic cream and liquid nitrogen to make its ice cream. At a cool 321 degrees below zero, the liquid nitrogen keeps fat and water molecules small, making for a creamier ice cream. 320 W. Third St., Suite D, Santa Rosa, 707-978-2635, dgicecream.com

Angela’s Ice Cream, Petaluma, Forestville and Healdsburg

Formerly known as Lala’s Creamery, this spot looks like the soda fountains of old, with a marble-topped bar and brick walls, but in addition to the traditional confections and banana splits, it serves up unique flavors. If you want to pair burgers with your ice cream, head on over to the Healdsburg location, home to Iggy’s Organic Burger. 134 Petaluma Blvd. N., Petaluma; 1390 N. McDowell Blvd., Petaluma; 6671 Front St., Forestville; 109 Plaza St., Healdsburg. angelasicecream.com

Fosters Freeze, Santa Rosa

This old-school burger and ice cream spot is all about the memories. Maybe because you’ve walked there, or your mom and dad took you in the family wagon – or it’s just Tuesday and you need a dip cone. 1400 Fourth St., Santa Rosa, 707-576-7028; 855 Sebastopol Road, Santa Rosa, 707-542-3212, fostersfreeze.com

Frozen Art, Santa Rosa

The Alcazars have been making Michoacana-style ice creams since 2011, originally as La Real Michoacana, and they continue to expand their lineup of 40-plus flavors. The menu includes Merlot chocolate chip, Kahlua, Mexican caramel, hibiscus flower, rum raisin and strawberry butter. The family comes from Tocumbo, Mexico’s ice cream-making capital. 500 Sebastopol Road, Suite B, Santa Rosa, 707-331-2899, frozenarticecream.com

Pink Sugar, Santa Rosa

Furry pink swings, a wall of shimmering pink mermaid scales, retro-style pink pay phones and pink velvet barstools make for an oh-so-Instagrammable moment at Pink Sugar, Santa Rosa’s favorite Thai rolled ice cream shop. Here’s how it works: Straus organic ice cream mix is poured onto chilled steel plates that almost instantly freeze it. Dual spatulas then chop, pulverize and blend in candy, cookies, fruit or cake before the mixture is spread into a thin layer and scraped into tight, frozen curls. Options include the Brookie, made with the standard vanilla base, fudge brownies, cookie dough and hot fudge; Cinnamon Toast Crunch with cinnamon toast cereal and caramel; and Banana Pudding with fresh bananas, caramel sauce and Nilla Wafers. 1224 Mendocino Ave., Santa Rosa. 707-368-3200, Instagram.com/pinksugarcreamery

Salt & Straw, Santa Rosa

The Portland, Oregon-based ice cream company is known for fearless flavor combinations: pear and blue cheese, Arbequina olive oil, strawberry honey balsamic with black pepper, or goat cheese with marionberries and habanero. Even its crowd-pleasers come with a twist, from vegan coconut mint chip and sea salt with caramel ribbons to fudgy brownie batter chocolate ice cream. At the start of each month, five limited-time themed flavors drop – always worth a taste, even if you’re not ready to commit to a full scoop of Gruyère and tomato custard tart. 700 Village Court at Montgomery Village, Santa Rosa, 707-360-6349, saltandstraw.com

La Michoacana, Sonoma

You can’t miss this ice cream spot’s bright pink and orange exterior. It’s best known for fruit paletas, or frozen ice pops. Try their Mangonada: blended fresh mango with ice, swirled chamoy sauce, topped with mango chunks and tamarind candy, and a tamarind stick. 18495 Highway 12, Sonoma, 707-938-1773, michoacana.com

Screamin’ Mimi’s, Sebastopol

It’s no surprise that Food & Wine magazine has named this Sebastopol ice cream spot one of the best in America. There’s always a line, there are always kids with messy chocolate grins and there’s always a new flavor to try. When it comes to rich dark chocolate, there’s always Mimi’s Mud or Deep Dark Secret. 6902 Sebastopol Ave., Sebastopol, 707-823-5902, screaminmimisicecream.com

Squatch’s Ice Cream and Coffee, Rohnert Park

This nonprofit ice cream and coffee shop near Sonoma State funds a nearby student center and serves up Petaluma’s own Mariposa ice cream. Find traditional scoops, milkshakes and Squatches — over-the-top ice cream sandwiches, like the popular Cookie Monster made with cookies-and-cream ice cream between chocolate chip cookies and rolled in mini M&Ms. 1451 Southwest Blvd., Suite 111, Rohnert Park, 707-992-0841, squatchscoffee.com

Sweet Scoops, Sonoma

Sonomans go wild for this housemade ice cream spot on the square, which always has fun, seasonal flavors, from simple vanilla to lemon custard and Mexican chocolate. Ice cream flavors rotate regularly; check their website or Instagram for current offerings. 408 First St. E., Sonoma, 707-721-1187, sweetscoopsicecream.com

Simply Scooped, Windsor

Ice cream tacos are the specialty: your go-to scoop, folded into a chocolate-dipped waffle cone. 9240 Redwood Highway, Windsor, 707-837-5965, thesimplyscooped.com

More favorites

Cielito Coffee and Ice Cream, Sonoma

This coffee and ice cream shop in the Vailetti Plaza shopping center on Highway 12 serves a wide variety of coffee beverages, milkshakes and ice cream. 205 Nino Marco Square, Sonoma, 707-343-7330, instagram.com/cielito_coffee_and_icecream

Fru-Ta, Santa Rosa and Petaluma

All natural flavors, both traditional and unconventional. Among the more unique are rose petal, guava, cheese, membrillo, chongo zamorano and mamey. Five locations in Santa Rosa and Petaluma, including an ice cream truck. frutaicecream.com

The Chocolate Cow, Sonoma

A Sonoma Plaza staple, Chocolate Cow scoops rich, creamy ice cream in classic and seasonal flavors, piled high into cones, cups and old-school sundaes. It’s the kind of place where kids press their noses to the glass and grown-ups suddenly remember why a double scoop always seemed like the right decision. 452 First St. E., Suite F, Sonoma, 707-935-3564, thechocolatecow.com

Honeymoon Frozen Yogurt, Sebastopol

This local yogurt shop is a favorite because of its organic ingredients and commitment to local farms. 7108 Bodega Ave., Sebastopol, 707-829-9866, honeymoonfrozenyogurt.com

Menchie’s Frozen Yogurt, Santa Rosa

The ultimate kid spot with over a dozen flavors like crème brûlée, mudslide pie, white chocolate raspberry and Dole Whip pineapple sorbet. 2188 Santa Rosa Ave., Santa Rosa, 707-545-9866, menchies.com

Noble Folk Ice Cream and Pie Bar, Santa Rosa and Healdsburg

This ice cream shop is worth a special trip. Unique flavors include Thai tea, cornflake maple, Dutch cookie and strawberry miso butterscotch, each inspired by local produce and the seasons. The menu changes frequently. 539 Fourth St., Santa Rosa, 707-978-3392; 116 Matheson St., Healdsburg, 707-395-4426, thenoblefolk.com

Petaluma Creamery, Petaluma

This historic creamery makes housemade ice cream along with Spring Hill cheese. Most popular is the lavender ice cream, but Meyer lemon is also a contender (pro tip: both work perfectly together). 711 Western Ave., Petaluma, 707-762-9038, springhillcheese.com

Swirl Time Frozen Yogurt Bar, Rohnert Park

Another locally owned Sonoma State fave serving up great fro-yo with a smile. 1718 E. Cotati Ave., Rohnert Park, 707-795-7900, swirltime.com

Two Dog Night Creamery, Sebastopol

Another instant-ice cream spot that uses organic local ingredients and natural flavors zapped with liquid nitrogen for soft, gelato-style ice cream. Seasonal flavors like matcha and brown butter are a treat, while classic scoops, including Dutch chocolate, banana Foster crunch and coffee Heath Bar, always satisfy. Don’t miss the floats, sundaes and milkshakes. At The Barlow, 6760 McKinley St., Suite 110, Sebastopol, 707-823-9376, twodognightcreamery.com

title: Michelin-Starred Restaurants in the Bay Area
summary:
Sonoma and Napa counties have an abundance of excellent restaurants. Here are the ones the Michelin Guide ranks supreme.

The post Michelin-Starred Restaurants in the Bay Area appeared first on Sonoma Magazine.
content:
The famed Michelin Guide has long been affirming what locals have known for years — the Bay Area is a food mecca. Residents and national publications alike rave about the area’s acclaimed chefs and their award-winning restaurants.

Sonoma County alone has an abundance of excellent restaurants, from fine dining bistros to casual community hubs. Some of our favorites earned stars in the recent 2026 Michelin Guide awards ceremony, including a new star for Troubadour in Healdsburg and a third star for Enclos in Sonoma.

Below are all the Michelin-starred restaurants in Sonoma and Napa counties, as well as the rest of the Bay Area.

Sonoma County

Three Stars

Enclos, Sonoma

Enclos had been eyeing a Michelin star since it opened in the fall of 2024. Last year, the Michelin Guide awarded it two stars for its “opulent tasting menu,” featuring locally sourced contemporary cuisine — becoming the first and only Michelin-starred restaurant in Sonoma. Enclos also received a green star, Michelin’s sustainability award. In June, Enclos received the rare third star. 139 E. Napa St, Sonoma, 707-387-1724, enclos-sonoma.com

SingleThread, Healdsburg

Repeatedly named among the world’s best restaurants, SingleThread retained its three Michelin stars for “exceptional cuisine.” It’s the only restaurant in Sonoma County with three stars. The farm-to-table restaurant also has a green star. Additionally, SingleThread’s five-room inn has three Michelin keys representing an extraordinary stay. 131 North St., Healdsburg, 707-723-4646, singlethreadfarms.com

One Star

Cyrus, Geyserville

Chef and author Douglas Keane reopened his Cyrus restaurant (formerly of Healdsburg) in Geyserville in 2022, and it promptly earned a Michelin star. 275 Highway 128, Geyserville, 707-723-5999, cyrusrestaurant.com

Troubadour, Healdsburg

Troubadour Bread & Bistro earned its first star in the 2026 Michelin awards, offering next-level bread and sandwiches by day and a multicourse tasting menu by night, when the boulangerie and sandwich shop turns into fine-dining restaurant Le Dîner. Owners Sean and Melissa McGaughey previously worked at the three-Michelin-starred SingleThread. 381 Healdsburg Ave., Healdsburg, 707-756-3972, troubadourhbg.com

Napa County

Three Stars

The French Laundry, Yountville

Despite recent lukewarm reviews, The French Laundry’s three Michelin stars, as well as its green star, were safe from the chopping block. It remains the only restaurant in Napa County with three stars. 6640 Washington St., Yountville, 707-944-2380, thomaskeller.com/tfl

One Star

Auberge du Soleil, Rutherford

Credited as Napa Valley’s first fine dining establishment, Auberge du Soleil has maintained its one Michelin star for 18 consecutive years, since the coveted guide was established in 2007. The restaurant’s hotel of the same name, part of the Auberge Resorts Collection, holds three Michelin keys. 180 Rutherford Hill Road, Rutherford, 800-348-5406, aubergeresorts.com/aubergedusoleil

Auro, Calistoga

Auro earned its one Michelin star in 2023, just eight months after opening. It’s located in Napa Valley’s Four Seasons Resort, which also has one Michelin key. 400 Silverado Trail N., Calistoga, 707-709-2160, auronapavalley.com

Press, St. Helena

Napa Valley’s Press restaurant earned its Michelin star in 2022 for its contemporary, Californian dishes. 587 St. Helena Highway, St. Helena, 707-967-0550, pressnapavalley.com

Mendocino County

Two Stars

Harbor House, Elk

This sustainable restaurant on the Mendocino Coast earned one Michelin star a year after opening — the county’s first Michelin star awarded in the inaugural 2019 Michelin Guide California. The second star came in 2021, recognizing chef Matthew Kammerer’s devotion to hyper-local, foraged ingredients and elevation of seafood delicacies. 5600 S. Highway 1, Elk, 707-877-3203, theharborhouseinn.com

Greater Bay Area

Three Stars

Atelier Crenn, 3127 Fillmore St., San Francisco, 415-440-0460, ateliercrenn.com

Benu, 22 Hawthorne St., San Francisco, 415-685-4860, benusf.com

Californios, 355 11th St., San Francisco, 415-757-0994, californiossf.com

Quince, 470 Pacific Ave., San Francisco, 415-775-8500, quincerestaurant.com

Two Stars

Acquerello, 1722 Sacramento St., San Francisco, 415-567-5432, acquerellosf.com

Birdsong, 1085 Mission St., San Francisco, 415-369-9161, birdsongsf.com

Californios, 355 11th St., San Francisco, 415-757-0994, californiossf.com

Commis, 3859 Piedmont Ave., Oakland, 510-653-3902, commisrestaurant.com

Kiln, 149 Fell St., San Francisco, 415-982-9722, kilnsf.com

title: How Troubadour Became Healdsburg’s Newest Michelin-Starred Restaurant
summary:
Chef Sean McGaughey built Michelin-starred Troubadour on his own terms, pairing French-inspired tasting menus with Run-DMC, thrifted china and plenty of fun.

The post How Troubadour Became Healdsburg’s Newest Michelin-Starred Restaurant appeared first on Sonoma Magazine.
content:
Healdsburg’s Troubadour has a shiny new Michelin star, awarded in June to the daytime sandwich shop and nighttime tasting-menu restaurant. That combination may be a headscratcher for some. To owners Sean and Melissa McGaughey, it makes perfect sense.

Both alumni of the three-Michelin-starred SingleThread, they have built a restaurant that upends convention, transforming a tiny daytime cafe into one of California’s newest Michelin-starred dining rooms.

“I’d tell people we’re a boulangerie in the morning, a sandwich shop by day and a fine-dining restaurant at night,” Sean McGaughey said. “And I’d get a ‘What?’”

The questions never threw him off course. A former punk-rock drummer who became a fine-dining chef before opening a bakery, McGaughey has never fit neatly into a culinary category. At Troubadour, he serves refined French-inspired cooking on thrifted Limoges china while Ludacris, Journey and Run-DMC play through the speakers.

“I think we’re wild cards, and we bring the fun,” he said.

The main event

In June, without any indication he was even under consideration, McGaughey received an invitation to the 2026 California Michelin Guide ceremony in San Diego. It seemed like a promising sign, but not a guarantee.

Even after making the trip with Melissa, the couple wasn’t convinced.

“We made it all the way down there, and it still felt like maybe we don’t have this,” he said.

They sat through the announcement of the year’s new one-star restaurants.

“It was agonizing,” McGaughey said. “But they’re not just going to make you sit in the chair of shame.”

Only when they walked onto the stage did the reality begin to sink in. Almost immediately, McGaughey found himself thinking about the so-called Michelin curse: higher expectations, greater demand and even more pressure.

“Every accolade,” he said, “can be a pat on the back and a punch in the stomach.”

That wariness comes from experience. McGaughey spent six formative years at Healdsburg’s SingleThread, joining early in its development and eventually becoming chef de cuisine under Kyle Connaughton.

Working alongside Kyle and Katina Connaughton and the opening team sharpened McGaughey’s technique and showed him how every detail fit into a larger vision. SingleThread quickly became one of the country’s most celebrated restaurants, earning three Michelin stars.

The accolades were thrilling, but they also revealed the demands of cooking at that level.

Fine dining on his own terms

By 2020, McGaughey was ready for a different pace. He and Melissa, a former SingleThread pastry chef, opened Quail & Condor Bakery after testing the concept at the Healdsburg Farmers Market and finding an enthusiastic audience.

“We were very much the new kids on the block,” he said. “When we started Quail, it was a small, ragtag thing, doing it our way however we could. We chose to keep it small and punk rock.”

Being a baker, however, doesn’t exactly mean banker’s hours. Bread, pastries and, later, sandwiches at Troubadour kept him busy, but they didn’t replace the satisfaction of composing a refined dish and watching a guest take the first bite.

He didn’t miss the pressures of fine dining. He missed the cooking.

This time, he decided, he would do it on his own terms: refined California cuisine built on French technique, using tradition as a point of departure rather than a rule book.

DIY fine dining

For the first two years of Troubadour’s day-to-night operation, McGaughey barely allowed himself to think about Michelin. He was too busy turning the couple’s sandwich shop into the restaurant he envisioned after dark: egg salad by day, morel-stuffed duck breast by night.

Early challenges were practical ones: installing a dimmer switch so dinner wasn’t served under interrogation lights and resetting the dining room after the lunch rush.

By 2024, as the French bistro concept found its footing, McGaughey and his team began thinking bigger. They dropped the prix fixe option so the kitchen could focus entirely on the tasting menu, and the unspoken dream gradually became an attainable goal.

Even then, McGaughey resisted building the restaurant around Michelin. Instead, he focused on creating the kind of place he wanted to eat in.

The backstory

McGaughey found his way into cooking much as he found punk rock, skateboarding and BMX biking: searching for places where outsiders could become insiders.

Growing up in Colorado, he discovered ambitious cooking through PBS’s “Great Chefs of the World,” long before celebrity chefs became television fixtures.

Restaurant kitchens quickly felt like home. They were loud, physical and fueled by adrenaline, bringing together people from different backgrounds to solve problems in real time.

A meal at The French Laundry showed him what cooking at the highest level could be. But it was the kitchen itself — the camaraderie, the pressure and the shared purpose — that kept pulling him deeper.

That path eventually led him to California and SingleThread.

During six years there, he refined his technique. More important, he said, he learned that ambitious cooking could remain collaborative, deeply personal and fun.

After the star

Weeks after receiving the Michelin star, McGaughey has had time to reflect.

So far, the award has brought more congratulations than complications.

“I feel like Healdsburg got that star, too,” he said.

A chef friend who struggled after earning a Michelin star offered advice that stuck with him: Michelin recognized Troubadour for what it already was. Don’t overhire. Don’t drain the bank account. Don’t reinvent the restaurant simply because someone handed it a star.

“That helped me digest it,” McGaughey said.

Now, the self-described cookbook nerd is focused on new recipes, old ideas and making the most of a kitchen barely large enough for three cooks. Water baths, low-temperature ovens and limited refrigeration compel the team to use every inch of space.

“It forces us to be creative and constantly change,” he said.

Thursday through Sunday, McGaughey and his team serve dishes such as duck breast with morels and dates, sea bream bouillabaisse, steak tartare with cured egg yolk and escargot served in a teacup.

“I’m not looking to be hoity-toity,” McGaughey said. “But cooking at the highest level is just fun.”

He still scours antique stores for rococo Limoges china — ornate pieces that are often too chipped or mismatched for serious collectors.

“I’m like a raven,” he said. “I just like shiny things. And the more gold, the better.”

Like the tiny cafe that earned a Michelin star, those overlooked plates have found new purpose in an unexpected setting.

Troubadour is at 381 Healdsburg Ave., Healdsburg. Lunch is served daily, dinner is by reservation only. The boulangerie is open 9 a.m. to 3 p.m. Monday through Sunday and Lé Diner is open 5:30-8:30 p.m. Thursday through Sunday. More details are available at troubadourhbg.com.

title: The Best Outdoor Dining Patios in Sonoma County
summary:
Slather on the sunscreen and settle in at these local outdoor dining destinations, where people come for the best food with a view.

The post The Best Outdoor Dining Patios in Sonoma County appeared first on Sonoma Magazine.
content:
Sonoma County can’t resist a good patio. With nearly year-round outdoor dining weather, we’re always looking for an alfresco option. Add an outdoor view and thoughtful menu, and everyone comes running. So slather on the sunscreen and settle in at these quiet favorites and buzzy newcomers to the open-air scene.

Best Bay Views

Fishetarian

Casual cove-side seating has always been part of the appeal at one of Bodega Bay’s favorite fish and chips spots, though tables disappear disappointingly fast on busy weekends. True to the restaurant’s “Bummer Free” motto, the owners recently renovated the adjacent fish house to add heated indoor seating and extra patio space with prime waterfront views to linger a little longer over fish tacos, crab cakes and gluten-free chowder. 599 Highway 1, Bodega Bay. 707-875-9092, fishetarianfishmarket.com

Best Riverside Views

Grand Central Petaluma

Tucked behind the Petaluma train station, this hidden gem offers casual waterside seating, roomy Adirondack chairs, a hammock, and communal tables. It’s an easy meet-up spot for playdates, brunches, and leisurely lunches over warm coffee and homemade empanadas. Tacos Don Pepe’s secret pop-up menu, available Friday through Sunday, is quietly gaining a loyal following. 226 Weller St., Petaluma. 707-774-6131, grandcentralpetaluma.com

Best Vista with a Beer

The Junction

The newly-opened beer garden sits high above Montgomery Drive at the former Villa restaurant. A 4,000-square-foot outdoor patio (with a playground) offers million-dollar vistas of nearby Annadel Park to enjoy while nibbling mushroom pizza, hot wings and sipping craft beer. Double the fun with cocktails and a screen-free arcade. Skee-Ball, anyone? 3901 Montgomery Drive, Santa Rosa. 707-800-7631, thejunc.com

Best Secret Spot

The Rooftop at Harmon Guest House

Seating is at a premium at this tiny rooftop hotel bar, but if you’re lucky enough to snag a table,  sweeping views of Fitch Mountain and a bird’s-eye view of the Healdsburg Plaza await. The limited menu is more happy hour than a three-course meal, but craft cocktails and nibbles like tuna tartare, truffle fries and tacos are top-notch. 227 Healdsburg Ave., Healdsburg. 707-922-5449, harmonguesthouse.com

Best Lake Views

Waterhawk Lake Club

Positioned along the edge of Roberts Lake, this sprawling Rohnert Park restaurant offers fire pits, shaded picnic tables, and breezy waterfront views ideal for everything from family dinners to cocktails and live music at sunset. Hot skillet artichoke dip, burgers and roasted carrots are favorite eats. 5000 Roberts Lake Road, Rohnert Park. 707-355-4219, thewaterhawk.com

Best Sunset

Andys Beeline Rooftop

Perched above Appellation Healdsburg, the sleek rooftop bar at Andys Beeline Rooftop pairs panoramic views with a floor-to-ceiling glass wall that catches every streak of orange, pink, and purple across the evening sky. Small bites from chef Charlie Palmer’s downstairs restaurant include smashburgers, okonomiyaki and a tinned fish board. Outdoor seats are coveted and reservations are highly recommended. 101 Dovetail Lane, Healdsburg. 707-723-2140, beelinerooftop.com

title: New Benevolent Neglect Wine Lounge Has a Secret Room, Groovy 1970s Look and Dance Parties
summary:
You don’t have to be young and hip to hang out at Benevolent Neglect — but a certain cool factor just might rub off on you if you do.

The post New Benevolent Neglect Wine Lounge Has a Secret Room, Groovy 1970s Look and Dance Parties appeared first on Sonoma Magazine.
content:
You don’t have to be young and hip to hang out at Benevolent Neglect — but a certain cool factor just might rub off on you if you do. The loungey tasting room is a relaxed and welcoming spot for sampling interesting, well-made wines crafted from familiar and under-the-radar grape varieties.

The story

Benevolent Neglect was hatched by friends Ben Brenner and Matt Nagy. Nagy became curious about wine after taking an appreciation class in college, while Brenner’s wine trajectory began in restaurants. Both men moved from Boston to Napa in the 2010s to pursue wine careers, with Nagy on the production side and Brenner in hospitality.

Nagy learned his way around cellars and vineyards working with some of Napa Valley’s most acclaimed winemakers, including Thomas Rivers Brown and Steve Matthiasson of Matthiasson Wines. Brenner also worked harvest jobs with Matthiasson before switching over to hosting tastings.

Nagy and Brenner became friends after meeting at a house party, and in 2013, they launched Benevolent Neglect — named as a nod to their less-is-more approach to winemaking. After nearly a decade building a cult-like following for their wines, the duo opened a tasting room in downtown Napa. In 2024, Jeff Warren joined the winery as a co-owner.

Benevolent Neglect’s lineup includes wines made from traditional and uncommon varieties — tried any Greco Bianco lately? — sourced from interesting growers across the state. Annual production is around 2,500 cases. When he’s not making wines for Benevolent Neglect, Nagy also works as a winemaker at Ashes & Diamonds in Napa.

The vibe

Benevolent Neglect is set in Napa’s funky SoFi district. Opened in 2022, the tasting room has a groovy, 1970s look thanks to retro lounge seating and wood paneling.

With vinyl spinning — and sometimes skipping — on the turntable and album covers displayed on the walls, music from Miles Davis to Bob Seger sets the tone. There’s even a secret room hidden behind a bookcase, used for special dinners and tastings. Always up for a good time, the winery sometimes co-hosts wine-centric dance parties with neighbors Gamling & McDuck and Maison Fayard.

On the palate

Instead of offering set flights, Brenner likes to tailor tastings for individual visitors. Before pouring anything into your glass, he’ll often take a minute to ask about preferences. Are you into crisp whites? Whole-cluster Syrahs? Want to try Counoise? Brenner and Nagy don’t refer to their wines as “natural” — they do use some sulfur to prevent spoilage — yet the wines lean in that direction, stylistically. They’re generally bright and clean, with alcohol levels on the lower side.

The 2024 Cemetery Road Pinot Grigio ($40) is made from Lodi grapes fermented on the skins. The effect is subtle, producing a textured wine with stone fruit flavors. A tribute to Cru Beaujolais, the oh-so-raspberry 2023 Gamay Noir from Carneros ($50) is a carbonic red with tons of berry fruit and plenty of acidity. The juicy 2021 Grenache from Alder Springs Vineyard in Mendocino County ($65) is silky and delicious, with a touch of green stemminess to offset the red berry fruit.

Tastings are $45 for five to six wines. A tasting experience in the secret back room is $110 per person for parties of two or more.

Beyond the bottle

Word has gotten out about La Cheve Bakery and Brews in Napa, but it’s still worth waiting in line. Set inside the Cayetano Juárez Adobe building — built well over a century ago — the family-owned café is a terrific stop for scratch-made pastries, all-day Mexican-style brunch, flavorful tacos and tortas, housemade beer, and a wine list showcasing local Hispanic winemakers.

Benevolent Neglect, 1417 Second St., Napa. Open noon to 6 p.m. Thursday through Sunday. 707-241-3463, bnwines.com

title: Get Ready for the Gravenstein Apple Fair in Sebastopol Aug. 8-9
summary:
Sebastopol’s beloved Gravenstein apple gets its annual celebration with fresh fritters, pies, cider, chef tastings and plenty of local food.

The post Get Ready for the Gravenstein Apple Fair in Sebastopol Aug. 8-9 appeared first on Sonoma Magazine.
content:
Oh, Gravenstein apple, how do we love thee? Thousands will count the ways Aug. 8-9 at the 53rd annual Gravenstein Apple Fair, when Sebastopol’s beloved sweet-tart mascot gets its moment in the sun — along with the fryer, pie tin and cider press.

Once a cornerstone crop in western Sonoma County, the heirloom Gravenstein is now more likely to be found in overgrown orchards and suburban front yards. The annual celebration at Ragle Ranch Regional Park honors the apple’s rich agricultural history — and its burgeoning future as a cider variety — with live music, family-friendly activities and plenty of apple-inspired food and drink. Proceeds benefit Sonoma County Farm Trails.

Apple Alley will be stocked with fresh-picked Gravensteins, towering pies, juice, apple butter, cider vinegar, caramels, apple-infused sauces and other orchard-made treats. Farm Trails volunteers will also fry the fair’s signature apple fritters to order — hot, crisp and worth the inevitable powdered-sugar shirt. Even the lines.

The apple pie baking contest returns Sunday, while caramel apple eating, apple juggling and apple balancing contests will take place throughout the weekend.

Local cider takes center stage in the Craft Cider Tent, with beer and wine also available throughout the festival grounds. Cold-pressed apple juice, lemonade, boba and other nonalcoholic drinks will be offered as well.

For a more leisurely experience, the advance-ticketed Artisan Tasting Grove features bites and sips from more than 30 local producers beneath the redwoods. Chef Bites pair local restaurants with artisan producers, including Handline with Heidrun Meadery, Bayou on the Bay with Hei Ma sauces, Rocker Oysterfeller’s with Liberty Ducks, and Goldfinch with Deer Valley Daughters and Sabi Greens.

Elsewhere on the grounds, vendors including Bayou on the Bay, A&M BBQ, Black Pig Meat Co., Gerard’s Paella, Marini’s Vegan BBQ, Mommy’s Yummys, Squatch’s Ice Cream, Tacos Don Pepe, Valley Ford Cheese & Creamery and Sonoma Family Meal’s Sabor Food Truck will serve heartier fare.

The Gravenstein Apple Fair runs from 10 a.m. to 6 p.m. Aug. 8 and 9 at Ragle Ranch Regional Park in Sebastopol. Advance admission is $23 for adults and $10 for children ages 6 to 12. Children 5 and younger are admitted free. Ticket prices increase after Aug. 7. Details are available at gravensteinapplefair.com.

title: A Return to Christo and Jeanne-Claude’s ‘Running Fence’ After 50 Years
summary:
Memories of the 1976 "Running Fence" art installation that changed Sonoma County’s landscape still resonate.

The post A Return to Christo and Jeanne-Claude’s ‘Running Fence’ After 50 Years appeared first on Sonoma Magazine.
content:
Imagine trying to tell the story of “Running Fence” to the uninitiated. It might go something like this: Back in the early 1970s, two little-known immigrant artists landed in rural west county like a pair of aliens descending from a UFO. Driving down gravel roads and knocking on ranch-house doors, they sat at kitchen tables sharing their bizarre vision of running an 18-foot-high white fabric fence 24 1/2 miles across dozens of ranches into the Pacific Ocean.

One by one, they began to convince ranchers this was a good idea. In countless community meetings, environmentalists, artists, and politicians quickly rose up in opposition. But the pair of outsiders persisted, and in 1976 after a four-year battle, Christo Vladimirov Javacheff and Jeanne-Claude Denat de Guillebon — or simply Christo and Jeanne-Claude — realized their pipe dream: A shimmering white nylon ribbon running across 59 ranches from Valley Ford to Bodega Bay for a grand total of two weeks. In a case of unlikely bedfellows, the artists’ biggest allies turned out to be the downhome ranchers who didn’t like environmentalists and big government telling them what they could do with their land.

Five decades later, it’s still hard to believe it really happened, and even harder to imagine something so ephemeral could last so long in the minds of those who witnessed it.

As both proof and paean to what transpired, the Museum of Sonoma County has mounted the landmark exhibition “Christo and Jeanne-Claude: Running Fence at 50 Years.” It includes fabric and poles from the original installation, Christo’s artwork, and a video re-creating how it billowed and rattled in the wind.

Curator Jennifer Bethke loves the backstory as much as the art itself. “I’m a total sucker for the people who were like, ‘It’s not art, it’s a curtain, right? It’s a roll of toilet paper.’ The controversy was fascinating to me,” she says.

Jeanne-Claude died in 2009 and Christo in 2020, but their vision lives on in the stories we continue to tell, long after the disassembled fence was donated to ranchers who used it to cover manure piles. They recast the poles as fencing, later giving away nylon panels that unfurled in a trail of fabric across the country, including from the rafters of the Monte Rio Theater.

The biggest epiphany was that it wasn’t just the fence that was the art: It was the theater of controversy, the conversations, and the consternation leading up to its installation. As Christo said at a particularly contentious meeting, “Like it or not, you are all a part of my art.”

Fifty years later, we’re still playing our roles, sharing stories and reflections. Union Hotel co-owner Barbara Gonnella, who grew up on Pozzi Ranch in Valley Ford, remembers it like it was yesterday. “It danced in the wind, and you could hear the poles whipping, especially on our ranch because it was very windy right before it cascaded into the Pacific. The sounds and the magic of the project were just timeless, but the friendships are even deeper. They’re as powerful as the art.”

Rumor has it there’s a 100-year time capsule buried near the Valley Ford Post Office. In 2076, when it’s pried open, there’s no doubt we’ll be buzzing about it all over again, playing our roles in the timeless art project that keeps running and running and running.

Christo and Jeanne-Claude: Running Fence at 50 Years

June 27 through Nov. 8 at Museum of Sonoma County. 425 Seventh St., Santa Rosa. museumsc.org

title: Local Chef’s ‘Hell Chicken’ Might Be a Taste of Heaven on Earth
summary:
How does chef Lee Desrosiers make his New York Times-recognized "Hell Chicken" so mind-blowingly delicious? The devil, as the saying goes, is in the details.

The post Local Chef’s ‘Hell Chicken’ Might Be a Taste of Heaven on Earth appeared first on Sonoma Magazine.
content:
Deep in the redwoods of west county, almond and oak smoke curls around the field kitchen chef Lee Desrosiers has parked at the end of his gravel driveway. The converted pig smoker is an amalgamation of grates, pipes, bricks, meat hooks, cast iron, and steel welded into a Frankencooker built for one very specific purpose: making his signature Hell Chicken.

Named for pollo alla diavola, the Italian name for an aggressively seasoned, spatchcocked chicken cooked over screaming-high heat, the title is more joke than homage—though the chickens might disagree.

Above hellfire-hot embers, whole birds hang from curved metal hooks, roasting slowly in a process powered by little more than salt, smoke, heat, and time. Desrosiers has spent more than a decade perfecting it, first on the East Coast and now in Sonoma County, where he’s made his home. What began as a weekend lark on a Brooklyn sidewalk has become a mission for the 42-year-old chef.

As fat renders and smoke drifts into the trees, Desrosiers works mostly by instinct, checking the coals and watching for the moment the skin tightens against the meat. Timing matters, but feel matters more.

His black Lab-Pit Bull mix, Frankie, knows the routine, circling the grill in hopes that gravity and good fortune might deliver an errant scrap, until a rustle in the tall grass sends her trotting into the weeds. Priorities.

She knows by smell that the chicken is nearly ready. What she doesn’t know is that I’m about to lose all objectivity over what may be the best chicken I’ll ever eat.

Brooklyn was where Desrosiers’ obsession with live-fire cooking first took shape. Already an accomplished chef, he landed there just as the borough’s artisanal food scene was exploding, fueled by the farm-to-table ethos of restaurants like Blue Hill, Superfine, and Marlow & Sons. He haunted farmers markets, learned to break down whole animals, and cooked in the stripped-down, ingredient-driven style that redefined dining from Austin to the Bay Area.

He spent a year working as a butcher at Achilles Heel, the Greenpoint gastropub where he’d eventually launch Hell Chicken, which gave him an intimate understanding of how muscle, fat, and connective tissue behave over heat, whether braised, grilled, or smoked.

On weekends, he would drag a grill into an empty parking space, first cooking chickens directly over hot coals before gradually jerry-rigging a setup that could smoke and braise them, too. Served half or whole with a simple salad, the dish felt ridiculously uncomplicated.

He kept refining the rig and fine tuning the bird, then in October 2016, The New York Times took notice. Suddenly, Desrosiers had an overnight poultry phenomenon on his hands.

“You are given forks and knives, but it’s hard to resist pulling off morsels of the golden skin with your fingers as if you were standing around in the kitchen at home,” critic Oliver Strand wrote. Within days, Desrosiers could barely cook fast enough to feed the crowds.

But California soon came calling. In 2018, he traded coasts after Scribe Winery offered him a job on its culinary team. Northern California wasn’t entirely new territory, however, and in some ways, it felt like a return.

“I happened upon Northern California on a post-college journey west, equal parts Kerouac and Bob Dylan, searching for some kind of gold, I guess,” says Desrosiers. “Half adventure, half accident, like so many Californians before me. Sonoma County has been that golden place for me.”

It was Sebastopol that won him over: a funky, rural pocket filled with orchards, towering redwoods, ocean air, and the kind of wide-open spaces a cramped Brooklyn parking spot could never offer. Having San Francisco’s eclectic restaurant scene just down the road didn’t hurt either.

The move gave Desrosiers room to evolve beyond the constraints of restaurant kitchens and parking space grilling. These days, he’s focused almost entirely on private events and live-fire cooking experiences, though he hints there may be more pop-ups in other cities ahead. His summer calendar is packed with birthdays, weddings, private dinners, and ticketed events across Sonoma County. At a single event, he may cook anywhere from a few dozen to more than 100 birds over a showstopper of a rig that resembles a Ferris wheel: Two towering 5-foot rings are connected by crossbars, enabling him to suspend chickens over an open fire pit like some kind of poultry carnival ride.

“It invites people into the cooking process,” he says. “The visual aspect of the whole thing is arresting and enchanting. Cooking usually happens behind closed doors. This provides connection.”

When it comes to what makes Desrosiers’ Hell Chicken so mind-blowingly delicious, the devil, as the saying goes, is in the details. He starts with Mary’s organic chicken, specifically the Freedom Ranger, a slower-growing bird than typical commercial broilers that are bred for oversized breasts and harvested at six-to-eight weeks. These birds have more balanced bodies and get nine-to-12 weeks to develop a fuller flavor, which Desrosiers says makes them especially suited to live-fire cooking.

The night before cooking, he dry rubs each bird—no secret seasonings— just salt, which results in juicy, deeply seasoned meat with extra-crispy skin. The next day, he hangs the chickens over embers until the skin tightens—usually 90 minutes to two hours—then transfers them to a Dutch oven banked with coals to braise in their own jus before moving them back to the grill to get crackling skin. It’s served with a squeeze of lemon and a pour of the concentrated braising juices, a sort of liquid gold that should probably be bottled and sold.

It all seems so utterly simple. Those hours of labor seem to evaporate the minute the meat hits the plate. Which is part of the point.

The drive to Desrosiers’ place is its own adventure, complete with GPS wrong turns, dirt roads, and wildlife darting through the brush. By the time I pull up, the smoke still perfumes the air. He’s set aside a private meal for us on the patio, beneath trees rustling in the afternoon wind. A still-warm chicken waits in a Dutch oven. Desrosiers hands me a spoon and gestures toward the jus beneath the bird, a glossy puddle of rendered fat and juices. It’s salty, concentrated, and oh-so-easy to eat straight from the pot.

A skillet of rice cooked in schmaltz arrives brown and crunchy at the edges, alongside charred cabbage with butter beans dressed in sauce made with green chile and preserved lemon that lands somewhere between pesto and chimichurri, but with more swagger than either. Slices of chicken, skin still glistening, come with broth to ladle over the top.

Flavors unfold gently with each bite: salt, umami, buttery skin, a flicker of char, a quiet note of smoke in the background. This is what chicken should taste like in a perfect world. And right now, that world feels pretty close.

Sitting at the table with Desrosiers has its own quiet magic. He’s humble and generous giving advice for his method, while knowing this is a meal mere mortals could never quite pull off at home. Somehow it feels deeply familiar, the kind of food that nudges at memories you’re not even sure belong to you. Frankie circles the table, tail wagging, still hoping for a bite. I’m happy to oblige, because some meals are better shared.

Hell Chicken might not be in every cook’s wheelhouse, but Lee Desrosiers’ recipe for grilled cabbage is an ideal, carefree side dish for grilling nights. It will pair well with most any protein you feel like making.

Grilled Cabbage with Preserved Lime and Chile

Makes 4 servings

  • 1 head of cabbage, see note
  • 1 tbsp. avocado oil
  • Kosher salt
For the sauce:
  • 2 serrano chiles, seeded and diced
  • 1/2 preserved lime (lemon also works well), rinsed and seeds removed
  • 1 tbsp. Colatura (anchovy sauce, or substitute fish sauce)
  • Juice of 2 limes (or lemons)
  • 1 tsp. white wine vinegar
  • 3 tbsp. olive oil

Cut the cabbage into quarters and set aside.

While grill heats, make the sauce.

In a food processor combine chiles, preserved lime, anchovy sauce, lime juice, and vinegar. Pulse a few times, and then with the motor running, drizzle in the olive oil until the mixture emulsifies. Alternatively, you can make the sauce in a bowl by finely dicing the chiles and preserved lime, then whisking in the remaining ingredients. Set sauce aside until it’s time to serve.

Meanwhile, toss the cabbage with the avocado oil and season with a healthy pinch of salt. Place cabbage cut side down on the grill, and grill over hot coals, or if using propane, over medium-high heat. Sear until the cabbage begins to caramelize and soften. Remove cabbage to a serving platter and spoon the sauce over it. Serve at once with your favorite grilled protein.

Note: Plan on 1/4 of a cabbage per person. The type of cabbage you use also determines how you should cook it. If using a tight head of cabbage, such as common red or green grocery store varieties, blanch the cabbage quarters in a pot of boiling water first. Remove from the pot, pat dry, and continue with the recipe. Loose-leaf cabbages like Savoy or the cone-shaped Caraflex can go straight on the grill.

title: Our Dining Editor’s Favorite Sonoma County Sweets Right Now
summary:
From chocolate croissants to soft serve, these are our favorite sweets in Sonoma County that are the perfect reason to eat dessert first.

The post Our Dining Editor’s Favorite Sonoma County Sweets Right Now appeared first on Sonoma Magazine.
content:
It always seems a shame to wait until after a meal to get a sweet treat — especially when you’re already full by the time the dessert menu comes around. These are the sugary delights that are the perfect reason to eat dessert first.

Raspberry White Chocolate Tart, Fleur Sauvage

It almost hurts to take the first bite of this oversized, raspberry-shaped beauty that gives the illusion of a plump berry fresh off the vine. But curiosity wins. Inside is a cloud of raspberry mousse with a bright pop of jelly at the center, perched on a white chocolate-filled tart. Pastry chef Robert Nieto, one of the world’s top chocolate and dessert talents, leans into the whimsy with two other versions — a cocoa pod filled with chocolate mousse and a faux mango layered with passion fruit and mango mousse. 370 Windsor River Road, Windsor. 707-892-2162, fleursauvagechocolates.com

Soft Serve, Valley Ford Creamery

Move over fro-yo, there’s a new cone in town. Valley Ford Creamery uses milk from its own Jersey cows for a gelato-smooth vanilla and chocolate soft serve worth a special trip to their café and cheese-aging facility. The herd’s high-fat milk gives this frozen treat a velvety texture that’s undeniably lickable. Grab a hunk of Estero Gold Reserve while you’re there because a sweet treat always needs a salty chaser. 14390 Valley Ford Road, Valley Ford. 707-875-7073, valleyfordcheese.com

Tres Leches Cake, Little Saint

It takes an ambitious pastry chef to make the traditional Mexican three milks cake without any dairy, but Dominick Miller-Luna has taken on the challenge, using coconut, soy, and oat milks to create a light, summery cake with a hint of lavender that’s entirely plant-based and gluten-free. There’s plenty of technique involved in mimicking heavy cream frosting with lentils, but Miller-Luna doesn’t let something like a lack of dairy slow him down a bit. 25 North St., Healdsburg. 707-433-8207, littlesainthealdsburg.com

It’s Not a Snickers Bar, Valette

As a kid, chef Dustin Valette’s dad was a sucker for frozen Snickers bars — the kind that could crack a tooth, he’s quick to point out. As an ode to pops, Valette and his brother Aaron created a pinkies-up riff on the milk chocolate, caramel and nuts classic, layering in burnt caramel, sea salt, cocoa nib tuile and peanut “snow.” The name is a tongue-in-cheek nod to possible trademark trouble, but a decade later, it’s still very much on the menu, to fans’ relief. 344 Center St., Healdsburg. 707-473-0946, valettehealdsburg.com

Gâteau Parisian, Patisserie Angelica

If you’re a fan of macarons, you’ll immediately be drawn to this naturally gluten-free upgrade. Instead of white flour, Gergana Karabelov uses almond flour to stack alternating layers of chewy macaron and praline buttercream. It’s decadent, with restrained sweetness, so the petite cake for one won’t tip into sugar overload — though you might side-eye anyone who asks for a bite. There’s a good reason it took top honors at the Sonoma County Harvest Fair. 6821 Laguna Park Way, Sebastopol. 707-827-7998, patisserieangelica.com

Strawberry Cups, Urban Deli

The Dubai chocolate trend might be yesterday’s news, but crackly knafeh and ripe strawberries smothered in chocolate and pistachio cream never go out of style. This version, served in a plastic cup (for easy travel), is messy and sticky in the best way possible. 151 Petaluma Blvd. S., Suite 109, Petaluma. 707-658-2183, eaturbandeli.com

Chef’s choice: Chocolate Croissant from Quail & Condor

Ryan Seal of The Sea Ranch Lodge

The new chef at Sonoma coast’s windswept Sea Ranch Lodge, Ryan Seal, spent his last few years working at the Greenwood Restaurant in Elk and family farm in Middletown. When he’s craving something sweet, Seal heads to Healdsburg for the shatteringly crisp chocolate scroll croissant with rich, dark chocolate batons from Dandelion Chocolate Factory. Mais oui! 44 Mill St., Unit J, Healdsburg. quailandcondor.com

title: 10 Cool Things To Do in Sonoma County When It’s Too Hot
summary:
Pull your head out of the freezer and check out these ways to beat the heat.

The post 10 Cool Things To Do in Sonoma County When It’s Too Hot appeared first on Sonoma Magazine.
content:
Sonoma County residents have a hot weekend ahead as the summer heat in the North Bay nears 100-degree temperatures. So how to stay cool? Keep reading and find out.

Head to the coast or the river

Notoriously cold during most of the year, Northern California beaches are the ultimate getaway for hot weather days. Pack a picnic and some sunblock and head out to Doran Beach in Bodega Bay, or any of our other favorite beaches. The Russian River has plenty of cool spots, too, like Johnson’s Beach in redwood-shaded Guerneville. Pro tip: Make your way to the beach early, before everyone else — and their cars — do the same. Johnson’s Beach in Guerneville has paddleboarding, picnicking, tubing and swimming. parks.sonomacounty.ca.gov, johnsonsbeach.com

Cool down under the canopy

Walk shaded by gentle giants in the Grove of Old Trees, perched high on a remote ridge top in Occidental. The grove is owned and managed by the land conservancy group LandPaths and includes 28 peaceful acres traversed by a network of wide, easy-to-walk trails. Access is free but be forewarned: There are no amenities, save for a picnic table. 17599 Fitzpatrick Lane, Occidental, 707-544-7284, landpaths.org

Armstrong Redwoods State Natural Reserve offers a year-round refuge for Sonoma County visitors and locals looking to get away from it all (parks.ca.gov). On hot days, it’s a good spot to cool down. Follow the paths meandering through the woods and take in the sounds of nature. Pro tip: Arrive early to enjoy the silence — sans selfie-snapping tourists on Segways. Then head to Nimble & Finn’s in downtown Guerneville for some cool, sweet scoops.

Get some ice cream

On meltingly hot days, thoughts turn to ice cream and its cousins — gelato and sorbet. Noble Folk Ice Cream and Pie Bar in Healdsburg and Santa Rosa is worth a special trip (thenoblefolk.com). Unique flavors include passion fruit, Thai tea, salted caramel and Dutch cookie, each inspired by local produce and the seasons. For more places to get a cool scoop, check here.

Keep the kids cool and happy

Take restless and overheated little ones to Snoopy’s Home Ice, or spend the day bowling, playing laser tag or jumping on the trampolines at Santa Rosa’s (air-conditioned) Poppy Bank Epicenter. Further north, play in the river at Healdsburg Veterans Memorial Beach.

Pair a movie with AC

Santa Rosa’s Airport Stadium 12 and Petaluma’s Boulevard 14 Cinema come with reclining chairs, beer and wine bars, and online ticket sales allowing moviegoers to choose their seats before getting to the theater. Pro tip: Get your tickets online before the heat peaks and then enjoy a movie and air conditioning.

Become a cave(wo)man for a day

Many Sonoma County wineries keep their wine barrels cool in underground caves, open to thirsty visitors looking to escape the heat. Head into the caves at Deerfield Ranch or Kunde Family Winery in Kenwood, for example. Pro tip: Reserve a tour or private tasting ahead of the heat wave — you won’t be the only one craving a caveman lifestyle once temperatures rise.

Or enjoy your wine with some AC

If you prefer to stay out of the cave but still crave some local vino, most Sonoma County tastings rooms are air conditioned. Not sure where to go? Check out these popular wineries for first-time visitors. Pro tip: In the heat, stick to whites and Pinot.

Rosé all day in the kiddie pool

Prefer to stay cool in the comfort of your own yard? Get an inflatable pool. Not just for the kiddos, you can get a slightly larger version just for you. Fill it up, then grab a bottle of your favorite Sonoma County rosé from the fridge. Pro tip: Add another splash of cool pink with rose sorbet, or a cute can of brut rosé.

Get cool in a bigger pool

If a small plastic pool isn’t cutting it for you, take the family to Morton’s Warm Springs in Kenwood, or get a massage and lounge by the mineral pool at the Fairmont Sonoma Mission Inn, a luxury hotel in Sonoma Valley. For more poolside wine sipping, there’s Francis Ford Coppola Winery in Geyserville (reservations required). Find more favorite local hotel pools here.

Hit the patio

Embrace the heat from underneath a patio umbrella, a cold drink in hand and a good meal on the table (find winery patios here; and outdoor dining here). Or cool down with a cocktail and a few nibbles at one of our favorite bars for hot summer nights.

Shana Bull and Maci Martell contributed to this article.

title: Where to Get the Best Ice Cream in Sonoma County
summary:
Whether it's hot, cold or somewhere in between, it's always a good time for ice cream. Here are the best places to get a cool, sweet scoop in Sonoma County.

The post Where to Get the Best Ice Cream in Sonoma County appeared first on Sonoma Magazine.
content:
Whether the weather’s hot, cold or somewhere in between, there’s never a bad time for ice cream. From swirls of soft serve and sorbet to traditional scoops and creamy custard, everyone’s got a favorite flavor.

Are you a strawberry waffle cone, lemon sorbet in a cup or chocolate and vanilla swirl in a cone? But the real question is, would you dare to eat pickle sorbet?

Whatever your choice, Sonoma County ice cream shops have you covered.

Top 15 Picks: Our Dining Editor’s Choices

Nimble & Finn’s, Santa Rosa and Guerneville

Cheeky by-the-scoop flavors include Front Porch Mint Chip (the mint is from one of the owner’s front porch), Meyer Lemon, Lavender Honeycomb and Whiskey Butterscotch. Can’t decide? Go for an eight-mini-scoop sampler. 16290 Main St., Guerneville, 707-666-9411; 123 Fourth St., Santa Rosa, 707-666-9590, nimbleandfinns.com

Goguette Bread, Santa Rosa

While known for their mélange of breads and pastries, Goguette also churns out delightful, French-style ice cream, or glacée. Using locally sourced or imported (from France and Italy) ingredients, find flavors like pear, lemon, chocolate orange, Madagascar vanilla and more. The bakery also sells ice cream cakes, with such flavors as vanilla, strawberry, pistachio and matcha. 59 Montgomery Drive, Santa Rosa, goguettebread.com

Handline, Sebastopol

This restaurant in Sebastopol was built on the site of an old Foster’s Freeze and the swirled chocolate and vanilla soft serve is still a favorite. Don’t miss the affogato, made with eye-opening cold brew and soft serve. 935 Gravenstein Highway S., Sebastopol, 707-827-3744, handline.com

Darling Ice Cream Shop, Sonoma

The ever-changing flavors at this charming Sonoma ice cream shop mean you’ll have plenty of reasons to return. A sister location to Sweet Scoops on the Sonoma Plaza, this neighborhood fave is known for its Watmaugh strawberry, salted caramel and, if you want to go the soft-serve route, a sunny Pineapple Dole Whip. 201 W. Napa St., Suite 6, Sonoma. 707-343-1482, darlingsonoma.com

Dave’s Gourmet Ice Cream, Santa Rosa

This local artisan producer uses premium organic milk, organic cream and liquid nitrogen to make its ice cream. At a cool 321 degrees below zero, the liquid nitrogen keeps fat and water molecules small, making for a creamier ice cream. 320 W. Third St., Suite D, Santa Rosa, 707-978-2635, dgicecream.com

Angela’s Ice Cream, Petaluma, Forestville and Healdsburg

Formerly known as Lala’s Creamery, this spot looks like the soda fountains of old, with a marble-topped bar and brick walls, but in addition to the traditional confections and banana splits, it serves up unique flavors. If you want to pair burgers with your ice cream, head on over to the Healdsburg location, home to Iggy’s Organic Burger. 134 Petaluma Blvd. N., Petaluma; 1390 N. McDowell Blvd., Petaluma; 6671 Front St., Forestville; 109 Plaza St., Healdsburg. angelasicecream.com

Fosters Freeze, Santa Rosa

This old-school burger and ice cream spot is all about the memories. Maybe because you’ve walked there, or your mom and dad took you in the family wagon – or it’s just Tuesday and you need a dip cone. 1400 Fourth St., Santa Rosa, 707-576-7028; 855 Sebastopol Road, Santa Rosa, 707-542-3212, fostersfreeze.com

Frozen Art, Santa Rosa

The Alcazars have been making Michoacana-style ice creams since 2011, originally as La Real Michoacana, and they continue to expand their lineup of 40-plus flavors. The menu includes Merlot chocolate chip, Kahlua, Mexican caramel, hibiscus flower, rum raisin and strawberry butter. The family comes from Tocumbo, Mexico’s ice cream-making capital. 500 Sebastopol Road, Suite B, Santa Rosa, 707-331-2899, frozenarticecream.com

Pink Sugar, Santa Rosa

Furry pink swings, a wall of shimmering pink mermaid scales, retro-style pink pay phones and pink velvet barstools make for an oh-so-Instagrammable moment at Pink Sugar, Santa Rosa’s favorite Thai rolled ice cream shop. Here’s how it works: Straus organic ice cream mix is poured onto chilled steel plates that almost instantly freeze it. Dual spatulas then chop, pulverize and blend in candy, cookies, fruit or cake before the mixture is spread into a thin layer and scraped into tight, frozen curls. Options include the Brookie, made with the standard vanilla base, fudge brownies, cookie dough and hot fudge; Cinnamon Toast Crunch with cinnamon toast cereal and caramel; and Banana Pudding with fresh bananas, caramel sauce and Nilla Wafers. 1224 Mendocino Ave., Santa Rosa. 707-368-3200, Instagram.com/pinksugarcreamery

Salt & Straw, Santa Rosa

The Portland, Oregon-based ice cream company is known for fearless flavor combinations: pear and blue cheese, Arbequina olive oil, strawberry honey balsamic with black pepper, or goat cheese with marionberries and habanero. Even its crowd-pleasers come with a twist, from vegan coconut mint chip and sea salt with caramel ribbons to fudgy brownie batter chocolate ice cream. At the start of each month, five limited-time themed flavors drop – always worth a taste, even if you’re not ready to commit to a full scoop of Gruyère and tomato custard tart. 700 Village Court at Montgomery Village, Santa Rosa, 707-360-6349, saltandstraw.com

La Michoacana, Sonoma

You can’t miss this ice cream spot’s bright pink and orange exterior. It’s best known for fruit paletas, or frozen ice pops. Try their Mangonada: blended fresh mango with ice, swirled chamoy sauce, topped with mango chunks and tamarind candy, and a tamarind stick. 18495 Highway 12, Sonoma, 707-938-1773, michoacana.com

Screamin’ Mimi’s, Sebastopol

It’s no surprise that Food & Wine magazine has named this Sebastopol ice cream spot one of the best in America. There’s always a line, there are always kids with messy chocolate grins and there’s always a new flavor to try. When it comes to rich dark chocolate, there’s always Mimi’s Mud or Deep Dark Secret. 6902 Sebastopol Ave., Sebastopol, 707-823-5902, screaminmimisicecream.com

Squatch’s Ice Cream and Coffee, Rohnert Park

This nonprofit ice cream and coffee shop near Sonoma State funds a nearby student center and serves up Petaluma’s own Mariposa ice cream. Find traditional scoops, milkshakes and Squatches — over-the-top ice cream sandwiches, like the popular Cookie Monster made with cookies-and-cream ice cream between chocolate chip cookies and rolled in mini M&Ms. 1451 Southwest Blvd., Suite 111, Rohnert Park, 707-992-0841, squatchscoffee.com

Sweet Scoops, Sonoma

Sonomans go wild for this housemade ice cream spot on the square, which always has fun, seasonal flavors, from simple vanilla to lemon custard and Mexican chocolate. Ice cream flavors rotate regularly; check their website or Instagram for current offerings. 408 First St. E., Sonoma, 707-721-1187, sweetscoopsicecream.com

Simply Scooped, Windsor

Ice cream tacos are the specialty: your go-to scoop, folded into a chocolate-dipped waffle cone. 9240 Redwood Highway, Windsor, 707-837-5965, thesimplyscooped.com

More favorites

Cielito Coffee and Ice Cream, Sonoma

This coffee and ice cream shop in the Vailetti Plaza shopping center on Highway 12 serves a wide variety of coffee beverages, milkshakes and ice cream. 205 Nino Marco Square, Sonoma, 707-343-7330, instagram.com/cielito_coffee_and_icecream

Fru-Ta, Santa Rosa and Petaluma

All natural flavors, both traditional and unconventional. Among the more unique are rose petal, guava, cheese, membrillo, chongo zamorano and mamey. Five locations in Santa Rosa and Petaluma, including an ice cream truck. frutaicecream.com

The Chocolate Cow, Sonoma

A Sonoma Plaza staple, Chocolate Cow scoops rich, creamy ice cream in classic and seasonal flavors, piled high into cones, cups and old-school sundaes. It’s the kind of place where kids press their noses to the glass and grown-ups suddenly remember why a double scoop always seemed like the right decision. 452 First St. E., Suite F, Sonoma, 707-935-3564, thechocolatecow.com

Honeymoon Frozen Yogurt, Sebastopol

This local yogurt shop is a favorite because of its organic ingredients and commitment to local farms. 7108 Bodega Ave., Sebastopol, 707-829-9866, honeymoonfrozenyogurt.com

Menchie’s Frozen Yogurt, Santa Rosa

The ultimate kid spot with over a dozen flavors like crème brûlée, mudslide pie, white chocolate raspberry and Dole Whip pineapple sorbet. 2188 Santa Rosa Ave., Santa Rosa, 707-545-9866, menchies.com

Noble Folk Ice Cream and Pie Bar, Santa Rosa and Healdsburg

This ice cream shop is worth a special trip. Unique flavors include Thai tea, cornflake maple, Dutch cookie and strawberry miso butterscotch, each inspired by local produce and the seasons. The menu changes frequently. 539 Fourth St., Santa Rosa, 707-978-3392; 116 Matheson St., Healdsburg, 707-395-4426, thenoblefolk.com

Petaluma Creamery, Petaluma

This historic creamery makes housemade ice cream along with Spring Hill cheese. Most popular is the lavender ice cream, but Meyer lemon is also a contender (pro tip: both work perfectly together). 711 Western Ave., Petaluma, 707-762-9038, springhillcheese.com

Swirl Time Frozen Yogurt Bar, Rohnert Park

Another locally owned Sonoma State fave serving up great fro-yo with a smile. 1718 E. Cotati Ave., Rohnert Park, 707-795-7900, swirltime.com

Two Dog Night Creamery, Sebastopol

Another instant-ice cream spot that uses organic local ingredients and natural flavors zapped with liquid nitrogen for soft, gelato-style ice cream. Seasonal flavors like matcha and brown butter are a treat, while classic scoops, including Dutch chocolate, banana Foster crunch and coffee Heath Bar, always satisfy. Don’t miss the floats, sundaes and milkshakes. At The Barlow, 6760 McKinley St., Suite 110, Sebastopol, 707-823-9376, twodognightcreamery.com

title: Michelin-Starred Restaurants in the Bay Area
summary:
Sonoma and Napa counties have an abundance of excellent restaurants. Here are the ones the Michelin Guide ranks supreme.

The post Michelin-Starred Restaurants in the Bay Area appeared first on Sonoma Magazine.
content:
The famed Michelin Guide has long been affirming what locals have known for years — the Bay Area is a food mecca. Residents and national publications alike rave about the area’s acclaimed chefs and their award-winning restaurants.

Sonoma County alone has an abundance of excellent restaurants, from fine dining bistros to casual community hubs. Some of our favorites earned stars in the recent 2026 Michelin Guide awards ceremony, including a new star for Troubadour in Healdsburg and a third star for Enclos in Sonoma.

Below are all the Michelin-starred restaurants in Sonoma and Napa counties, as well as the rest of the Bay Area.

Sonoma County

Three Stars

Enclos, Sonoma

Enclos had been eyeing a Michelin star since it opened in the fall of 2024. Last year, the Michelin Guide awarded it two stars for its “opulent tasting menu,” featuring locally sourced contemporary cuisine — becoming the first and only Michelin-starred restaurant in Sonoma. Enclos also received a green star, Michelin’s sustainability award. In June, Enclos received the rare third star. 139 E. Napa St, Sonoma, 707-387-1724, enclos-sonoma.com

SingleThread, Healdsburg

Repeatedly named among the world’s best restaurants, SingleThread retained its three Michelin stars for “exceptional cuisine.” It’s the only restaurant in Sonoma County with three stars. The farm-to-table restaurant also has a green star. Additionally, SingleThread’s five-room inn has three Michelin keys representing an extraordinary stay. 131 North St., Healdsburg, 707-723-4646, singlethreadfarms.com

One Star

Cyrus, Geyserville

Chef and author Douglas Keane reopened his Cyrus restaurant (formerly of Healdsburg) in Geyserville in 2022, and it promptly earned a Michelin star. 275 Highway 128, Geyserville, 707-723-5999, cyrusrestaurant.com

Troubadour, Healdsburg

Troubadour Bread & Bistro earned its first star in the 2026 Michelin awards, offering next-level bread and sandwiches by day and a multicourse tasting menu by night, when the boulangerie and sandwich shop turns into fine-dining restaurant Le Dîner. Owners Sean and Melissa McGaughey previously worked at the three-Michelin-starred SingleThread. 381 Healdsburg Ave., Healdsburg, 707-756-3972, troubadourhbg.com

Napa County

Three Stars

The French Laundry, Yountville

Despite recent lukewarm reviews, The French Laundry’s three Michelin stars, as well as its green star, were safe from the chopping block. It remains the only restaurant in Napa County with three stars. 6640 Washington St., Yountville, 707-944-2380, thomaskeller.com/tfl

The restaurant’s hotel of the same name, part of the Auberge Resorts Collection, holds three Michelin keys. 180 Rutherford Hill Road, Rutherford, 800-348-5406, aubergeresorts.com/aubergedusoleil

Auro, Calistoga

Auro earned its one Michelin star in 2023, just eight months after opening. It’s located in Napa Valley’s Four Seasons Resort, which also has one Michelin key. 400 Silverado Trail N., Calistoga, 707-709-2160, auronapavalley.com

The second star came in 2021, recognizing chef Matthew Kammerer’s devotion to hyper-local, foraged ingredients and elevation of seafood delicacies. 5600 S. title: How Troubadour Became Healdsburg’s Newest Michelin-Starred Restaurant
summary:
Chef Sean McGaughey built Michelin-starred Troubadour on his own terms, pairing French-inspired tasting menus with Run-DMC, thrifted china and plenty of fun.

The post How Troubadour Became Healdsburg’s Newest Michelin-Starred Restaurant appeared first on Sonoma Magazine.
content:
Healdsburg’s Troubadour has a shiny new Michelin star, awarded in June to the daytime sandwich shop and nighttime tasting-menu restaurant. That combination may be a headscratcher for some. To owners Sean and Melissa McGaughey, it makes perfect sense.

Both alumni of the three-Michelin-starred SingleThread, they have built a restaurant that upends convention, transforming a tiny daytime cafe into one of California’s newest Michelin-starred dining rooms.

“I’d tell people we’re a boulangerie in the morning, a sandwich shop by day and a fine-dining restaurant at night,” Sean McGaughey said. “And I’d get a ‘What?’”

The questions never threw him off course. A former punk-rock drummer who became a fine-dining chef before opening a bakery, McGaughey has never fit neatly into a culinary category. At Troubadour, he serves refined French-inspired cooking on thrifted Limoges china while Ludacris, Journey and Run-DMC play through the speakers.

“I think we’re wild cards, and we bring the fun,” he said.

The main event

In June, without any indication he was even under consideration, McGaughey received an invitation to the 2026 California Michelin Guide ceremony in San Diego. It seemed like a promising sign, but not a guarantee.

Even after making the trip with Melissa, the couple wasn’t convinced.

“We made it all the way down there, and it still felt like maybe we don’t have this,” he said.

They sat through the announcement of the year’s new one-star restaurants.

“It was agonizing,” McGaughey said. “But they’re not just going to make you sit in the chair of shame.”

Only when they walked onto the stage did the reality begin to sink in. Almost immediately, McGaughey found himself thinking about the so-called Michelin curse: higher expectations, greater demand and even more pressure.

“Every accolade,” he said, “can be a pat on the back and a punch in the stomach.”

That wariness comes from experience. McGaughey spent six formative years at Healdsburg’s SingleThread, joining early in its development and eventually becoming chef de cuisine under Kyle Connaughton.

Working alongside Kyle and Katina Connaughton and the opening team sharpened McGaughey’s technique and showed him how every detail fit into a larger vision. SingleThread quickly became one of the country’s most celebrated restaurants, earning three Michelin stars.

The accolades were thrilling, but they also revealed the demands of cooking at that level.

Fine dining on his own terms

By 2020, McGaughey was ready for a different pace. He and Melissa, a former SingleThread pastry chef, opened Quail & Condor Bakery after testing the concept at the Healdsburg Farmers Market and finding an enthusiastic audience.

“We were very much the new kids on the block,” he said. “When we started Quail, it was a small, ragtag thing, doing it our way however we could. We chose to keep it small and punk rock.”

Being a baker, however, doesn’t exactly mean banker’s hours. Bread, pastries and, later, sandwiches at Troubadour kept him busy, but they didn’t replace the satisfaction of composing a refined dish and watching a guest take the first bite.

He didn’t miss the pressures of fine dining. He missed the cooking.

This time, he decided, he would do it on his own terms: refined California cuisine built on French technique, using tradition as a point of departure rather than a rule book.

DIY fine dining

For the first two years of Troubadour’s day-to-night operation, McGaughey barely allowed himself to think about Michelin. He was too busy turning the couple’s sandwich shop into the restaurant he envisioned after dark: egg salad by day, morel-stuffed duck breast by night.

Early challenges were practical ones: installing a dimmer switch so dinner wasn’t served under interrogation lights and resetting the dining room after the lunch rush.

By 2024, as the French bistro concept found its footing, McGaughey and his team began thinking bigger. They dropped the prix fixe option so the kitchen could focus entirely on the tasting menu, and the unspoken dream gradually became an attainable goal.

Even then, McGaughey resisted building the restaurant around Michelin. Instead, he focused on creating the kind of place he wanted to eat in.

The backstory

McGaughey found his way into cooking much as he found punk rock, skateboarding and BMX biking: searching for places where outsiders could become insiders.

Growing up in Colorado, he discovered ambitious cooking through PBS’s “Great Chefs of the World,” long before celebrity chefs became television fixtures.

Restaurant kitchens quickly felt like home. They were loud, physical and fueled by adrenaline, bringing together people from different backgrounds to solve problems in real time.

A meal at The French Laundry showed him what cooking at the highest level could be. But it was the kitchen itself — the camaraderie, the pressure and the shared purpose — that kept pulling him deeper.

That path eventually led him to California and SingleThread.

During six years there, he refined his technique. More important, he said, he learned that ambitious cooking could remain collaborative, deeply personal and fun.

After the star

Weeks after receiving the Michelin star, McGaughey has had time to reflect.

So far, the award has brought more congratulations than complications.

“I feel like Healdsburg got that star, too,” he said.

A chef friend who struggled after earning a Michelin star offered advice that stuck with him: Michelin recognized Troubadour for what it already was. Don’t overhire. Don’t drain the bank account. Don’t reinvent the restaurant simply because someone handed it a star.

“That helped me digest it,” McGaughey said.

Now, the self-described cookbook nerd is focused on new recipes, old ideas and making the most of a kitchen barely large enough for three cooks. Water baths, low-temperature ovens and limited refrigeration compel the team to use every inch of space.

“It forces us to be creative and constantly change,” he said.

Thursday through Sunday, McGaughey and his team serve dishes such as duck breast with morels and dates, sea bream bouillabaisse, steak tartare with cured egg yolk and escargot served in a teacup.

“I’m not looking to be hoity-toity,” McGaughey said. “But cooking at the highest level is just fun.”

He still scours antique stores for rococo Limoges china — ornate pieces that are often too chipped or mismatched for serious collectors.

“I’m like a raven,” he said. “I just like shiny things. And the more gold, the better.”

Like the tiny cafe that earned a Michelin star, those overlooked plates have found new purpose in an unexpected setting.

Troubadour is at 381 Healdsburg Ave., Healdsburg. Lunch is served daily, dinner is by reservation only. The boulangerie is open 9 a.m. to 3 p.m. Monday through Sunday and Lé Diner is open 5:30-8:30 p.m. Thursday through Sunday. More details are available at troubadourhbg.com.

title: The Best Outdoor Dining Patios in Sonoma County
summary:
Slather on the sunscreen and settle in at these local outdoor dining destinations, where people come for the best food with a view.

The post The Best Outdoor Dining Patios in Sonoma County appeared first on Sonoma Magazine.
content:
Sonoma County can’t resist a good patio. With nearly year-round outdoor dining weather, we’re always looking for an alfresco option. Add an outdoor view and thoughtful menu, and everyone comes running. So slather on the sunscreen and settle in at these quiet favorites and buzzy newcomers to the open-air scene.

Best Bay Views

Fishetarian

Casual cove-side seating has always been part of the appeal at one of Bodega Bay’s favorite fish and chips spots, though tables disappear disappointingly fast on busy weekends. True to the restaurant’s “Bummer Free” motto, the owners recently renovated the adjacent fish house to add heated indoor seating and extra patio space with prime waterfront views to linger a little longer over fish tacos, crab cakes and gluten-free chowder. 599 Highway 1, Bodega Bay. 707-875-9092, fishetarianfishmarket.com

Best Riverside Views

Grand Central Petaluma

Tucked behind the Petaluma train station, this hidden gem offers casual waterside seating, roomy Adirondack chairs, a hammock, and communal tables. It’s an easy meet-up spot for playdates, brunches, and leisurely lunches over warm coffee and homemade empanadas. Tacos Don Pepe’s secret pop-up menu, available Friday through Sunday, is quietly gaining a loyal following. 226 Weller St., Petaluma. 707-774-6131, grandcentralpetaluma.com

Best Vista with a Beer

The Junction

The newly-opened beer garden sits high above Montgomery Drive at the former Villa restaurant. A 4,000-square-foot outdoor patio (with a playground) offers million-dollar vistas of nearby Annadel Park to enjoy while nibbling mushroom pizza, hot wings and sipping craft beer. Double the fun with cocktails and a screen-free arcade. Skee-Ball, anyone? 3901 Montgomery Drive, Santa Rosa. 707-800-7631, thejunc.com

Best Secret Spot

The Rooftop at Harmon Guest House

Seating is at a premium at this tiny rooftop hotel bar, but if you’re lucky enough to snag a table,  sweeping views of Fitch Mountain and a bird’s-eye view of the Healdsburg Plaza await. The limited menu is more happy hour than a three-course meal, but craft cocktails and nibbles like tuna tartare, truffle fries and tacos are top-notch. 227 Healdsburg Ave., Healdsburg. 707-922-5449, harmonguesthouse.com

Best Lake Views

Waterhawk Lake Club

Positioned along the edge of Roberts Lake, this sprawling Rohnert Park restaurant offers fire pits, shaded picnic tables, and breezy waterfront views ideal for everything from family dinners to cocktails and live music at sunset. Hot skillet artichoke dip, burgers and roasted carrots are favorite eats. 5000 Roberts Lake Road, Rohnert Park. 707-355-4219, thewaterhawk.com

Best Sunset

Andys Beeline Rooftop

Perched above Appellation Healdsburg, the sleek rooftop bar at Andys Beeline Rooftop pairs panoramic views with a floor-to-ceiling glass wall that catches every streak of orange, pink, and purple across the evening sky. Small bites from chef Charlie Palmer’s downstairs restaurant include smashburgers, okonomiyaki and a tinned fish board. Outdoor seats are coveted and reservations are highly recommended. 101 Dovetail Lane, Healdsburg. 707-723-2140, beelinerooftop.com
