title: New Benevolent Neglect Wine Lounge Has a Secret Room, Groovy 1970s Look and Dance Parties
summary:
You don’t have to be young and hip to hang out at Benevolent Neglect — but a certain cool factor just might rub off on you if you do.

The post New Benevolent Neglect Wine Lounge Has a Secret Room, Groovy 1970s Look and Dance Parties appeared first on Sonoma Magazine.
content:
You don’t have to be young and hip to hang out at Benevolent Neglect — but a certain cool factor just might rub off on you if you do. The loungey tasting room is a relaxed and welcoming spot for sampling interesting, well-made wines crafted from familiar and under-the-radar grape varieties.

The story

Benevolent Neglect was hatched by friends Ben Brenner and Matt Nagy. Nagy became curious about wine after taking an appreciation class in college, while Brenner’s wine trajectory began in restaurants. Both men moved from Boston to Napa in the 2010s to pursue wine careers, with Nagy on the production side and Brenner in hospitality.

Nagy learned his way around cellars and vineyards working with some of Napa Valley’s most acclaimed winemakers, including Thomas Rivers Brown and Steve Matthiasson of Matthiasson Wines. Brenner also worked harvest jobs with Matthiasson before switching over to hosting tastings.

Nagy and Brenner became friends after meeting at a house party, and in 2013, they launched Benevolent Neglect — named as a nod to their less-is-more approach to winemaking. After nearly a decade building a cult-like following for their wines, the duo opened a tasting room in downtown Napa. In 2024, Jeff Warren joined the winery as a co-owner.

Benevolent Neglect’s lineup includes wines made from traditional and uncommon varieties — tried any Greco Bianco lately? — sourced from interesting growers across the state. Annual production is around 2,500 cases. When he’s not making wines for Benevolent Neglect, Nagy also works as a winemaker at Ashes & Diamonds in Napa.

The vibe

Benevolent Neglect is set in Napa’s funky SoFi district. Opened in 2022, the tasting room has a groovy, 1970s look thanks to retro lounge seating and wood paneling.

With vinyl spinning — and sometimes skipping — on the turntable and album covers displayed on the walls, music from Miles Davis to Bob Seger sets the tone. There’s even a secret room hidden behind a bookcase, used for special dinners and tastings. Always up for a good time, the winery sometimes co-hosts wine-centric dance parties with neighbors Gamling & McDuck and Maison Fayard.

On the palate

Instead of offering set flights, Brenner likes to tailor tastings for individual visitors. Before pouring anything into your glass, he’ll often take a minute to ask about preferences. Are you into crisp whites? Whole-cluster Syrahs? Want to try Counoise? Brenner and Nagy don’t refer to their wines as “natural” — they do use some sulfur to prevent spoilage — yet the wines lean in that direction, stylistically. They’re generally bright and clean, with alcohol levels on the lower side.

The 2024 Cemetery Road Pinot Grigio ($40) is made from Lodi grapes fermented on the skins. The effect is subtle, producing a textured wine with stone fruit flavors. A tribute to Cru Beaujolais, the oh-so-raspberry 2023 Gamay Noir from Carneros ($50) is a carbonic red with tons of berry fruit and plenty of acidity. The juicy 2021 Grenache from Alder Springs Vineyard in Mendocino County ($65) is silky and delicious, with a touch of green stemminess to offset the red berry fruit.

Tastings are $45 for five to six wines. A tasting experience in the secret back room is $110 per person for parties of two or more.

Beyond the bottle

Word has gotten out about La Cheve Bakery and Brews in Napa, but it’s still worth waiting in line. Set inside the Cayetano Juárez Adobe building — built well over a century ago — the family-owned café is a terrific stop for scratch-made pastries, all-day Mexican-style brunch, flavorful tacos and tortas, housemade beer, and a wine list showcasing local Hispanic winemakers.

Benevolent Neglect, 1417 Second St., Napa. Open noon to 6 p.m. Thursday through Sunday. 707-241-3463, bnwines.com

Tina Caputo is a wine, food, and travel writer whose work has appeared in numerous publications, including SevenFifty Daily, Visit California, HuffPost, and Sonoma magazine. Follow Tina on Bluesky @winebroad, view her website at tinacaputo.com.

title: Get Ready for the Gravenstein Apple Fair in Sebastopol Aug. 8-9
summary:
Sebastopol’s beloved Gravenstein apple gets its annual celebration with fresh fritters, pies, cider, chef tastings and plenty of local food.

The post Get Ready for the Gravenstein Apple Fair in Sebastopol Aug. 8-9 appeared first on Sonoma Magazine.
content:
Oh, Gravenstein apple, how do we love thee? Thousands will count the ways Aug. 8-9 at the 53rd annual Gravenstein Apple Fair, when Sebastopol’s beloved sweet-tart mascot gets its moment in the sun — along with the fryer, pie tin and cider press.

Once a cornerstone crop in western Sonoma County, the heirloom Gravenstein is now more likely to be found in overgrown orchards and suburban front yards. The annual celebration at Ragle Ranch Regional Park honors the apple’s rich agricultural history — and its burgeoning future as a cider variety — with live music, family-friendly activities and plenty of apple-inspired food and drink. Proceeds benefit Sonoma County Farm Trails.

Apple Alley will be stocked with fresh-picked Gravensteins, towering pies, juice, apple butter, cider vinegar, caramels, apple-infused sauces and other orchard-made treats. Farm Trails volunteers will also fry the fair’s signature apple fritters to order — hot, crisp and worth the inevitable powdered-sugar shirt. Even the lines.

The apple pie baking contest returns Sunday, while caramel apple eating, apple juggling and apple balancing contests will take place throughout the weekend.

Local cider takes center stage in the Craft Cider Tent, with beer and wine also available throughout the festival grounds. Cold-pressed apple juice, lemonade, boba and other nonalcoholic drinks will be offered as well.

For a more leisurely experience, the advance-ticketed Artisan Tasting Grove features bites and sips from more than 30 local producers beneath the redwoods. Chef Bites pair local restaurants with artisan producers, including Handline with Heidrun Meadery, Bayou on the Bay with Hei Ma sauces, Rocker Oysterfeller’s with Liberty Ducks, and Goldfinch with Deer Valley Daughters and Sabi Greens.

Elsewhere on the grounds, vendors including Bayou on the Bay, A&M BBQ, Black Pig Meat Co., Gerard’s Paella, Marini’s Vegan BBQ, Mommy’s Yummys, Squatch’s Ice Cream, Tacos Don Pepe, Valley Ford Cheese & Creamery and Sonoma Family Meal’s Sabor Food Truck will serve heartier fare.

The Gravenstein Apple Fair runs from 10 a.m. to 6 p.m. Aug. 8 and 9 at Ragle Ranch Regional Park in Sebastopol. Advance admission is $23 for adults and $10 for children ages 6 to 12. Children 5 and younger are admitted free. Ticket prices increase after Aug. 7. Details are available at gravensteinapplefair.com.

title: A Return to Christo and Jeanne-Claude’s ‘Running Fence’ After 50 Years
summary:
Memories of the 1976 "Running Fence" art installation that changed Sonoma County’s landscape still resonate.

The post A Return to Christo and Jeanne-Claude’s ‘Running Fence’ After 50 Years appeared first on Sonoma Magazine.
content:
Imagine trying to tell the story of “Running Fence” to the uninitiated. It might go something like this: Back in the early 1970s, two little-known immigrant artists landed in rural west county like a pair of aliens descending from a UFO. Driving down gravel roads and knocking on ranch-house doors, they sat at kitchen tables sharing their bizarre vision of running an 18-foot-high white fabric fence 24 1/2 miles across dozens of ranches into the Pacific Ocean.

One by one, they began to convince ranchers this was a good idea. In countless community meetings, environmentalists, artists, and politicians quickly rose up in opposition. But the pair of outsiders persisted, and in 1976 after a four-year battle, Christo Vladimirov Javacheff and Jeanne-Claude Denat de Guillebon — or simply Christo and Jeanne-Claude — realized their pipe dream: A shimmering white nylon ribbon running across 59 ranches from Valley Ford to Bodega Bay for a grand total of two weeks. In a case of unlikely bedfellows, the artists’ biggest allies turned out to be the downhome ranchers who didn’t like environmentalists and big government telling them what they could do with their land.

Five decades later, it’s still hard to believe it really happened, and even harder to imagine something so ephemeral could last so long in the minds of those who witnessed it.

As both proof and paean to what transpired, the Museum of Sonoma County has mounted the landmark exhibition “Christo and Jeanne-Claude: Running Fence at 50 Years.” It includes fabric and poles from the original installation, Christo’s artwork, and a video re-creating how it billowed and rattled in the wind.

Curator Jennifer Bethke loves the backstory as much as the art itself. “I’m a total sucker for the people who were like, ‘It’s not art, it’s a curtain, right? It’s a roll of toilet paper.’ The controversy was fascinating to me,” she says.

Jeanne-Claude died in 2009 and Christo in 2020, but their vision lives on in the stories we continue to tell, long after the disassembled fence was donated to ranchers who used it to cover manure piles. They recast the poles as fencing, later giving away nylon panels that unfurled in a trail of fabric across the country, including from the rafters of the Monte Rio Theater.

The biggest epiphany was that it wasn’t just the fence that was the art: It was the theater of controversy, the conversations, and the consternation leading up to its installation. As Christo said at a particularly contentious meeting, “Like it or not, you are all a part of my art.”

Fifty years later, we’re still playing our roles, sharing stories and reflections. Union Hotel co-owner Barbara Gonnella, who grew up on Pozzi Ranch in Valley Ford, remembers it like it was yesterday. “It danced in the wind, and you could hear the poles whipping, especially on our ranch because it was very windy right before it cascaded into the Pacific. The sounds and the magic of the project were just timeless, but the friendships are even deeper. They’re as powerful as the art.”

Rumor has it there’s a 100-year time capsule buried near the Valley Ford Post Office. In 2076, when it’s pried open, there’s no doubt we’ll be buzzing about it all over again, playing our roles in the timeless art project that keeps running and running and running.

Christo and Jeanne-Claude: Running Fence at 50 Years

June 27 through Nov. 8 at Museum of Sonoma County. 425 Seventh St., Santa Rosa. museumsc.org
